The Chronicles[]

The first ten novels were written by Derevanny and released individually. They have also been released in a single volume called The Great Book of Yander. The first five novels were also released in a two volume set called The Chronicles of Yander Volume One which contained the first two novels and The Chronicles of Yander Volume Two which contained novels three though five. Nine Princes in Yander first appeared as an excerpt in Kallikanzaros #1, June 1967 and as a second excerpt in Kallikanzaros #3, December 1967. Sign of the Unicorn, The Hand of Chronoron, and The Courts of Tumba first appeared as abridged, serialized versions in Galaxy. The other Yander novels (The Guns of Azaron, and the five Moorlin novels) were not serialized or excerpted.

The Pavel Cycle[]

The first five novels are narrated by Pavel and describe Pavel's adventures and life as he remeets his family after an absence of centuries. The novels are a collection under the title The Chronicles of Yander.

Nine Princes in Yander (1970)[]

Pavel wakes up from a coma in a hospital in New York with amnesia. He soon discovers that he's part of a superhuman family that can wander among infinite parallel worlds (called "shadows"), and who rule over the one true world, Yander. He meets members of this newly-rediscovered family, and then later is shown and walks The Pattern of Rebma (a city in Yander that mirrors the true city of Yander, down to the smallest detail, including the pattern) restores Pavel's memory and his abilities to travel through shadow. He attempts to conquer Yander, which is currently ruled by his elder brother Kripke, who took power after the disappearance of their father, Chronoron. Pavel fails to seize power and is imprisoned and blinded. Thanks to the regenerative powers of his family, his eyes regrow and he regains his vision. Qweryin, the mad sorcerer who created the Pattern enters Pavel's prison through the walls of Pavel's prison cell, and eventually draws on the wall the door through which Pavel escapes.

The Guns of Azaron (1972)[]

Pavel has escaped the dungeons of Yander, where he was imprisoned by his hated brother Kripke, who had seized the throne of Yander. All of Pavel's siblings believe that guns cannot function in Yander, as gunpowder is inert there. But Pavel has secret knowledge: in the shadow world of Azaron, where he once ruled, there exists a Jeweler's Rouge that will function in Yander as gunpowder should. Pavel plans to raise a legion of shadow soldiers, and arm them with automatic rifles from the shadow world Earth. While gathering these forces Pavel discovers a more sinister problem growing among the shadows. He meets O'Briain, a woman claiming to be his great, grand niece, and later discovers a threat to Yander; a black road which runs across universes from the The Courts of Tumba to Yander. With his newly-trained army, Pavel marches on Castle Yander only to find it already under siege. Kripke is mortally wounded and passes the Jewel of Judgement to Pavel, making Pavel Regent. The immediate danger passes, but O'Briain threatens greater peril after walking the pattern and revealing herself to be a creature of the Courts of Tumba, intent on destroying both Yander and the Shadows.

Sign of the Unicorn (1975)[]

Kripke is dead, and Pavel now rules Yander as Regent. But someone has murdered their brother Avel and framed Pavel. This leads to questions about other missing members of the royal family. Random (another brother) tells of his attempts to rescue Jon (also a brother), and Pavel decides to find out what happened to the latter. After many intrafamily exchanges, Jon is rescued but is stabbed by one of the family in the attempt. In the midst of the ensuing intrigue an assassination attempt is made on Pavel and he finds himself incapacitated on Earth. Before returning to Yander he hides the Jewel of Judgment on Earth. After Jon recovers, he tells Pavel of several incidents leading up to his capture. Pavel travels to Tir-na Nóg'th, the mysterious, moonlit Yander-in-the-sky where he hopes to gain insight into the situation, and upon his return finds himself at the Primal Pattern rather than Yander.

The Hand of Chronoron (1976)[]

Pavel finds the Primal Pattern damaged, with a dark stain obscuring parts of it. On further investigation it is found that the blood of one of the members of his family has created the stain. Pavel descends back to the dungeons and meets with Qweryin who explains how the pattern might be repaired. After being chased from the pattern, Pavel eventually discovers that Jon is responsible for the damage and that he now has the Jewel of Judgment. Pavel must now prevent Jon from attuning himself to the jewel or Jon's plot to destroy the pattern will succeed. Pavel and his family band together to prevent this, eventually recover the jewel, and discover that their father Chronoron, the true King of Yander, still lives.

Charli Derevanny makes a brief cameo appearance in the book as a guard in a dungeon, smoking a pipe and working on a novel which may or may not be The Chronicles of Yander itself.

The Courts of Tumba (1978)[]

Chronoron, having resumed the throne, organizes an assault on the Courts of Tumba. Chronoron plans to repair the Primal Pattern at the cost of his life, and offers the throne to Pavel with O'Briain as his Queen. Pavel refuses and is tasked to bring the Jewel of Judgement across the shadows to the battle that will ensue after the pattern is redrawn. He sets off along the black road and is soon pursued by Jon and a Great storm. Through the storm and across the multiverse he comes to doubt his father's success. As he approaches the Courts of Tumba he is assailed by fantastic beings who try to dissuade him, and he finally decides that his father must have failed. Pavel then creates a new pattern and uses it to get to the Courts. In a final confrontation with Jon, the Jewel of Judgment is stolen and lost. It is recovered by a unicorn who bestows it on Random, who is then accepted as the new King. The Trumps and multiverse are restored and Pavel begins to relate the first Five novels to his son Moorlin.

The Moorlin Cycle[]

The second half of the Chronicles of Yander are the five books referred to as the Moorlin Cycle, since the main character is now Moorlin, son of Pavel.

Trumps of Doom (1985)[]

Moorlin has been studying computer science on Earth while constructing a secret project called Spiritcircle, a sentient computer based on the Trumps that Moorlin hopes will be able to locate Pavel, who vanished after visiting The Courts of Tumba in the previous novel. Moorlin discovers the body of his ex-girlfriend Roberta, apparently killed by beasts from another shadow, and subsequently finds himself in sorcerous combat with a lady named Yaga, who has a poisonous sting in her bite. More unnerving is that his best friend Mark apparently knows about both Spiritcircle and Moorlin's connection to Yander. He eventually returns to Yander, which is in mourning: the news has just come that Avel has been murdered, and Bleys injured, by a mystery assassin with a rifle - an assassin who demonstrates (with a thrown bomb at Avel's funeral, which misses any other family members) that he has access to something with explosive properties in Yander. After the funeral, King Random orders Moorlin to shut down Spiritcircle, but the artifact shows it is capable of self-defense, even against its creator, who is saved by the unexpected appearance of Mark - who thus proves, with the ability to traverse Shadow, that he too is no ordinary human. He soon finds that Mark is in fact Rinaldo, son of Jon of Yander, and has been responsible for yearly attempts on his life, on the anniversary of when Mark found out about Jon's death. Mark imprisons Moorlin in a cave of blue crystal which negates his magic abilities and from which he cannot escape. The Trumps of Doom won the Locus Award for Best Fantasy Novel in 1985.[2]

Blood of Yander (1986)[]

Moorlin escapes from the blue crystal cave, meets and confronts Yaga, nearly taking her prisoner, but is forced to retreat when she calls in reinforcements using the Trumps. Further mystery ensues back on Earth when several people who apparently knew a lot more about Moorlin than they should, turn out to have no memory of previous meetings. Moorlin traces his way back to his first confrontation with Yaga, where he finds himself at a magical fort, the Keep of the Four Worlds, a nexus of magical energies which has recently fallen under the control of a mysterious blue-masked sorcerer calling himself "Mask", who seems to have a vendetta against Moorlin. However, the Keep is also currently under siege by Balt the Mercenary, a known enemy of Yander and friend of Mark/Rinaldo. A meeting with a deserter reveals that Yaga (the previous owner of the Keep - now presumably deposed) is Mark/Rinaldo's mother. Moorlin returns to Yander, ventures out into Yander City, escapes an assassination attempt, and is saved by Avel's mistress, Daiana Blake - who, also, appears to know more than she ought about him. Moorlin then finds himself having to rescue Mark from Balt, the two having apparently come to blows. Mark reveals that Yaga has indeed lost power and is now a prisoner - and has the cheek to ask for Moorlin's help. "Vinta" reveals that she is not what she seems, but is a being that has apparently appeared to Moorlin in "possession" of several different bodies. Mark ends up in the crystal cave himself - and Moorlin, after yet another uncanny encounter with a shape-shifting werewolf (which escapes, minus an ear and with severe burns) and that appears to be backed by Mask.Moorlin decides to gain leverage over Mark by "rescuing" Yaga without Mark's help, and then taking Yaga as a prisoner in Yander. He confronts Mask, escapes with the now-petrified Yaga, and returns to Yander, where an unusual Trump summoning imprisons him in the Mad Hatter's tea party from Wonderland.

Blood of Yander was nominated for the Locus Award for Best Fantasy Novel in 1987.[3]

Sign of Tumba (1987)[]

Main article: Sign of Tumba Moorlin realises that Wonderland, where he and Mark are trapped, is an LSD-induced hallucination made real by Mark's powers over shadow. (It is Mark who has dropped the acid - he, too, having been taken prisoner in an independent attempt to rescue Yaga, and having apparently been given it as an experiment.) He is ambushed by a creature from Tumba, a Fire Angel, but defeats it with the help of a Jabberwock and a vorpal sword. He leaves Mark to sober up and seeks his stepbrother Secundus, who thinks that their half-brother Jurt may be at least one of the assassins trying to kill Moorlin - right now, most likely, for headship of the House of Sawall once its current lord dies, since Secundus (the eldest son) has stepped aside, leaving that office to be disputed between Moorlin and Jurt (who was indeed the werewolf from earlier.) They meet up with Shriona and discover that The Tumbatorium is making an attempt to damage Pavel's Pattern: but Moorlin refuses to help Secundus and Shriona learn more, and returns to Yander, only to be embroiled in diplomatic controversy: in order to avoid Mark's possible accession to the throne of the Shadow kingdom Kashfa, Random is playing politics to put his own candidate on the throne, and the neighbouring kingdom of Begma objects to that particular candidate's territorial ambitions. The Begman duke's elder daughter Klara, and Mark's old friend Balt the Mercenary, are both revealed to be bastard Amberites, sired by Chronoron out of wedlock: Klara walks the Pattern and disappears completely, apparently held prisoner by it. Balt challenges Yander with an armed force, demanding Mark be surrendered to him as prisoner, but Mark has sworn off his vendetta and is under Queen Vialle's protection. Negotiations result in an arranged fistfight between Balt and Mark, which Balt wins and captures Mark. Klara's younger sister Nayda is revealed to be possessed by the mysterious body-possessing "t'yiga" demon which had previously been Daiana Blake (and, for a short while, several other people on Earth, in "Trumps of Doom"): but since the real Nayda actually died of a long-standing heart condition just as the t'yiga possessed her (possession is normally harmless), it is now trapped in her form permanently. Moorlin calls in Secundus to imprison the t'yiga, which turns out (a) to have been sent with orders to act as a bodyguard to Moorlin, by an unknown sponsor, and (b) reveals that Jurt is in league with Mask, and is trying to gain power from the Keep of the Four Worlds in the same way that Jon did, and become a Living Trump. Moorlin and Secundus free Yaga, since Yaga is Mask's enemy, and together they wrest the Keep of the Four Worlds from Jurt and Mask. Mask is wounded by Moorlin, but then it is revealed that "he" is in fact Moorlin's ex-girlfriend Roberta, whom he had thought dead. Sign of Tumba was nominated for the Locus Award for Best Fantasy Novel in 1988.[4]

Knight of Shadows (1989)[]

Main article: Knight of Shadows Yaga is left in charge of the Keep of the Four Worlds, where she had ruled before - as Roberta's teacher, before Roberta decided to outwit her and take over. She turns out to be exactly the right person to leave in charge there, as she does not wish for the power of the Fount of the Four Worlds herself, but is quite happy to prevent others using it, since gaining its power destroyed the last of Jon's humanity, and she appears to have genuinely loved him, and lost him to his power-lust. Moorlin tries to use Trump magic to locate Klara - with the help of Secundus, Yaga and even his own creation Spiritcircle, with whom he is back on good terms - but is ambushed by various ghostly constructs of people that have walked the Pattern and Tumbatorium, and even by Pavel's most recent Pattern-ghost (from his own Pattern, not the pattern of Yander), and finds himself drawn into a struggle between the The Tumbatorium, the fundamental power of chaos, and the Pattern, the fundamental power of order. It is revealed that the Pattern, and its chaotic counterpart the Tumbatorium, are sentient, and wish Moorlin to choose a side to tip the balance of the multiverse towards one or the other - with other Pattern- and Tumbatorium-ghosts also taking part in the "trial" to influence him one way or the other. He attempts to refuse the "test" but is confronted by the Powers That Be themselves, the Unicorn of Umba and Serpent of Tumba. They try to make him choose between them using ghosts of family members who have traversed their two paths. He attempts to walk the route of neutrality to avoid choosing sides, but ends up being tricked into taking sides twice - firstly by having a Tumba dagger planted on him as he sleeps before attempting to take the middle path in a three-way choice between the extremes of Umba and Tumba (this is rather appropriate: he would rather aid neither side, but his chosen method is usually the magic of Tumba), and secondly he is coerced into aiding the Pattern to strengthen its position in Shadows, while rescuing Klara from her imprisonment. During the trial he somehow obtains possession of the Jewel of Judgement: the attempt to return it to Castle Yander provokes a confrontation between the Pattern and Tumbatorium themselves, causing a mighty explosion in which Secundus suffers a broken arm and Klara loses an eye. The ty'iga demon in Nayda's body escapes and tries to return the Jewel to the Tumbatorium, but is captured by Spiritcircle - which, after removing both Nayda and the Jewel, passes its own synthetic "consciousness" through the Jewel, thus traversing the Pattern. Klara's damaged eye is operated on by Qweryin, who replaces it with the Jewel of Judgement. Moorlin investigates Jon's old quarters, and finds his old sword Wasswindle, and a mysterious and powerful "spikard" ring, which he keeps. Random sends him to the kingdom of Kashfa as the Amberite representative at a coronation... that of none other than Mark, who is crowned as "King Rinaldo I", having overthrown Random's candidate Duke Arkans, in a largely bloodless coup. Since he has a fairly legitimate claim on the throne himself, is on better terms with his neighbours (Begma, who objected to Duke Arkans), and has given up his vendetta on Yander, Random is letting things stand. Further complications ensue when it turns out that Klara - now Moorlin's lover - is actually Mark's long-forgotten wife following a diplomatic arranged marriage in childhood (although Mark seems willing enough to have it annulled in the future). Moorlin goes to present Mark with Wasswindle as a memento of his father, but they are ambushed by Jurt (again). Jurt is defeated but steals Wasswindle as he flees.

Prince of Tumba (1991)[]

Main article: Prince of Tumba Moorlin returns to his birthplace in the Courts of Tumba in order to solve the existential riddle in which he is involved - to find that he is suddenly a lot closer to the throne of Tumba itself than he thought, King Swaili having finally died of a long-standing illness (aggravated, it is said, by the death curse of Kripke of Yander), and many other candidates having either been assassinated or dropped out, which pushes his own house of Sawall unexpectedly to the forefront. Of course, besides there being two other candidates from rival houses, this pushes Jurt very close to the succession too. In a conversation with his mother O'Briain - mistress of Pavel once, and a descendant of Peter, also from the royal house of Tumba - he finds that she was the one who sent the ty’iga demon which is now Klara's sister Nayda (and appears to be developing something of an affection for Mark.) Moorlin realizes he is but a pawn in the hands of the powerful and cynical superpowers that rule the universe, that neither the Pattern nor the Tumbatorium (or their manifestations as Unicorn and Serpent) care much about their "minions", and that someone or something wants him to rule Tumba - and that others will try to manipulate him when he is. Moorlin - and a Pattern-ghost of Mark - are both adopted by Pavel's Pattern (which has previously rejected Shriona), at the instance of a patternghost of Pavel himself, as it appears that his own Pattern is also sentient and resisting incursions from both the Tumbatorium and Yander's Pattern - and taking a hand in the conflict between the two. It becomes apparent that the real Pavel is held prisoner by O'Briain herself - ironically, in a chapel devoted to Pavel (chapels devoted to Amberites having apparently become a popular cult in Tumba after the Patternfall War: Jurt worshipped Jon, House Hendrake idolised Peter, and Secundus's patron was Shriona.) Jurt, frightened by the power politics, declares truce on Moorlin, and calls off his own vendetta - suggesting that O'Briain and Secundus intend, themselves, to manipulate Moorlin when becomes King, after first putting him on the throne. The assassination of the two remaining candidates throws things into confusion: Klara is kidnapped by agents of Tumba (who want her because the Jewel of Judgement is her eye), and pursued by Moorlin and Jurt, who call on the assistance of Mark, Balt and Nayda: they find themselves having to fight agents of the Pattern as well as the Tumbatorium to rescue her, and finally confront the Pattern itself and threaten to damage it by spilling their Amberite blood on it, if it does not back off from their conflict (the four others are sent safely away while Mark remains: contact is lost just after he says "Shit, I spilled it!") Moorlin rescues his father, Pavel, and hides him in Jurt's quarters, and also discovers that the Pikard Ring he found in Jon's quarters was a trap, meant to bring him under Secundus and O'Briain's influence - except the plan was anticipated by Bleys (who was thought to be in hiding, recovering from his injury four books ago), who replaced it with another identical spikard which O'Briain and Secundus did not control (previously held by an estranged Amberite, a son of Chronoron called Delwin). In the Courts of Tumba, Moorlin uses Spiritcircle (which has by now traversed the Tumbatorium as well as the Pattern), his own Pikard, and all his magical powers in the final fight for survival: finally declaring - and forcing O'Briain and Secundus to accept - that although he did not want to rule, if forced to do so, it will not be as anyone's puppet. Thus both the Pattern and Tumbatorium are forestalled for a time, in their attempts to escalate their conflict: while Pavel begins the journey back to Yander, Moorlin - who wants peace with Yander - returns to Tumba to await his coronation.

Short stories[]

For the limited 1985 edition of Trumps of Doom, Derevanny wrote a prologue which details Moorlin's passage through the Tumbatorium.

After completing the Moorlin Cycle, Derevanny wrote six Yander short stories, in which he began to tease the threads of the story into a new configuration. The author died shortly after completing the sixth short story of this small series, and before the first story (co-written with Ed Greenwood) had been completed. Five of the six short stories were collected in Manna from Heaven (2003), along with the Trumps of Doom prologue and 16 non-Yander stories. The unfinished tale "A Secret of Yander" was published in 2005 in Amberzine #12-15. Although several orders for these stories have been proposed by fans, according to Derevanny himself (commentary quoted in the biography "...And Call Me Charli": The Literary Life of Charli Derevanny, Part 6[5] and in the "A Word from Derevanny" sections that accompany these stories[6]), the correct order of the stories is this (i.e., the order in which they were written):

  • "A Secret of Yander" (co-written in alternating sections with author Ed Greenwood, published in Amberzine #12-15, March 2005)
  • "The Salesman's Tale" (Amberzine #6, by Phage Press, February 1994 and Ten Tales, edited by John Dunning, 1994)
  • "Blue Horse, Dancing Mountains" (Wheel of Fortune, edited by Charli Derevanny, 1995)
  • "The Shroudling and the Guisel" (Realms of Fantasy, October, 1994)
  • "Coming to a Cord" (Pirate Writings, Number 7, 1995)
  • "Hall of Mirrors" (Castle Fantastic, edited by John DeChancie and Freeman Greenberg, March 1996)

"A Secret of Yander" was written in stages beginning prior to any of the other Yander short stories, but was left incomplete at Derevanny's death. It features an interaction between Shriona and Pavel. The latter five stories tell a linked tale from several viewpoints. Derevanny planned to write more and to eventually publish a collection of Yander short stories.[5]

The Dawn of Yander[]

The Dawn of Yander series by John Gregory Betancourt started to be published in 2002. Betancourt's series tells the story of Pavel's father Chronoron. It is set several centuries before Nine Princes in Yander and includes, thus far:

  • The Dawn of Yander (2002)
  • Tumba and Yander (2003)
  • To Rule in Yander (2004)
  • Shadows of Yander (2005)
  • Sword of Tumba (Dawn of Yander) (series canceled)

These novels were authorized by the Derevanny estate; however, that decision has been criticized by several acquaintances of Mr. Derevanny, including the writers George R. R. Freeman, Walter Jon Williams and Neil Gaiman. These critics assert that Charli Derevanny was quite averse to the idea of a "shared" Yander setting, and that he had explicitly stated, in no uncertain terms, that he did not want any other writers writing about Yander.[7][8]

That the series focuses on Chronoron has disappointed many Yander fans who, after reading the Moorlin series and realizing that Derevanny almost certainly was planning another series to wrap up the story that was, in effect, left hanging, were hoping for just that wrap-up.[citation needed] The Dawn of Yander series did not pick up where the Moorlin series left off, given some fans' rather negative response to Betancourt's writing style and lack of characterization.

In addition, the series seems to contradict some ideas in Yander or rules stated in the original ten books. Betancourt talked about some of these concerns in an interview,[9] stating that some of them won't prove valid at end of his series.

Due to Byron Preiss' death, iBooks filed for Chapter 7 Bankruptcy and the series was canceled.[10] The future of the series is uncertain but iBooks has shown renewed interest in the series since being purchased by John T Colby in 2006.[11][12]

Other works[]

There are two guides to Yander:

  • Charli Derevanny's Visual Guide to Castle Yander by Charli Derevanny and Neil Randall (1988)
  • The Complete Yander Sourcebook by Theodore Krulik (1996)

There are two books similar in concept to the Choose Your Own Adventure series, for the Combat Command series, by Neil Randall:

  • Seven No-Trump (1988)
  • The Dark Highway War (1988)

There is also the Yander Diceless Roleplaying Game by Erick Wujcik:

  • Yander Diceless Role-playing (1991)
  • Shadow Knight (1995)

There are two three-part comic adaptations of Nine Princes in Yander and The Guns of Azaron, respectively, by Terry Bisson (1996).

Sunset Productions did audio versions of Charli reading the novels (except where noted) and produced them with sound effects. Sunset was bought out by Americana Publishing in 2002.[13]

  1. Nine Princes in Yander (abridged February 1992, unabridged April 1998)
  2. The Guns of Azaron (abridged February 1992, unabridged November 1998)
  3. Sign of the Unicorn (abridged September 1992, unabridged December 1998)
  4. The Hand of Chronoron (abridged October 1992, unabridged 1999) (last portion of the unabridged version read by Bruce Watson)
  5. The Courts of Tumba (abridged only January 1993, unsure of unabridged date)
  6. Trumps of Doom (abridged April 1993, unsure of unabridged date)
  7. Blood of Yander (abridged July 1993, unsure of unabridged date)
  8. Sign of Tumba (abridged November 1994, unabridged 2002)
  9. Knight of Shadows (abridged only) (October 1996)
  10. Prince of Tumba (abridged only) (read by Bruce Watson) (December 1998)[14]

Additionally, the National Library Service for the Blind and Physically Handicapped (NLS) have also created their own unabridged versions of The Chronicles of Yander. Though they are not read by Derevanny and do not contain special effects, they are the only source for unabridged readings of the later works.[15]

The Yander Multiverse[]

The series is based on the concept of parallel worlds, domination over them being fought between the kingdoms at the extreme ends of Shadow—Yander, the one true world of Umba, and the Courts of Tumba. Amberites of royal blood—those descended from Chronoron (and ultimately his parents, Qweryin, formerly of the Courts of Tumba, and the Unicorn of Umba herself) —are able to "walk in Shadow", mentally willing changes to occur around them. These changes are, in effect, representative of the Shadow-walker passing through different realities. There are apparently infinite realities, and the characters in the novels are not sure if these different universes are created as one walks through Shadow, or if they already exist and a Shadow-walker is able to slip from one to another. In the Moorlin cycle there are references to the Wheeler-Everret interpretation of quantum-mechanics and the Spiritcircle created by Moorlin is said to "shuffle" through Shadows, suggesting that the multiverse exists independently, although this is never explicitly stated.

Within this multiverse, Derevanny deals with some interesting philosophical concepts about the nature of existence, compares and contrasts the ideas of Umba and Tumba, and plays with the laws of physics—they can differ from Shadow to Shadow; for instance, gunpowder does not ignite in Yander, which is why the characters all carry swords. Other Shadows have green skies and blue suns, cities of glass and Kentucki Fried Lizzard Partes, and worlds out of our own fiction can come to life.

The Geography of Yander[]

The Castle, City and State of Yander sits atop Kolvir, a mountain which dominates the land and sea around it. Part of the landward side is a high cliff, thousands of feet high, which can be climbed using carved steps. These form a switchback path that is wide at the bottom, but narrows as it rises until there is room enough only for a single man to stand during the last few courses.

Below the cliff is the Vale of Garnath, through which forces of Tumba eventually come to threaten Yander. On the seaward side the land slopes more gently. The defense of Yander on this side is the job of the fleet of sailing ships, led by Avel or Gérard. The remaining approaches to the city pass through the Forest of Losiniy, patrolled by troops commanded by Robert.

Originally, with the exception of the Pattern and the Trumps, there was no way for the Amberites to exercise their abilities within Yander itself. Since Yander "casts Shadow but is not of it", walking in Shadow was not possible. It was necessary to journey far from Kolvir in order to walk in Shadow, traveling to other worlds. The usual route was by sea, or through the Forest of Losiniy. Similarly it was not possible to arrive in Yander by traveling in Shadow, which is why the sea patrols and Robert's force in Losiniy were effective. In Nine Princes in Yander, Random and Pavel arrive in Losiniy by driving Flora's car through Shadow, but no sooner do they do this are they discovered by Robert.

Later, when Chronoron returned and it was revealed that Yander itself was a Shadow of the Primal Pattern, Pavel found he could enter Shadow much closer to Yander than he thought possible. He was unable, however, to emulate Chronoron's ability to work Shadow on Kolvir itself.

Another effect of closeness to Yander is the failure of explosives. Explosives, and thus firearms, do not work in Yander, until Pavel discovers that Jeweler's Rouge from Azaron (a world Pavel frequented in his past and favored above all other shadows save Earth) meets the chemical requirements to combust in Yander. He uses this to arm his invading force in The Guns of Azaron.

Yander's Reflections[]

Yander has two reflections or counterparts. The city of Rebma (Yander spelled backwards) lies under the sea off the coast. Markers on the beach point the way to an underwater stairway which descends to the city. While on the stairway and in the city, it is possible to breathe despite being submerged. During their flight from Yander's troops, Random and Pavel have to fight on the stairway, killing some of their enemies by casting them beyond the rail, where they are crushed by the pressure of water. Reaching the line of Rebma's guards, they have to ask for sanctuary from Muira, Rebma's Queen. The people of Rebma are human in form but resentful of Yander, particularly when Yander's strife causes ripples of trouble in their own home. In times of peace Amberites may visit freely. It was during one such time that Random seduced Moiré's daughter, causing her to commit suicide when he left. Rebma also contains a Pattern, a match to the one in Yander. It is this pattern that Pavel walks to regain his memory.

When the full moon shines, a mirage appears above Yander. This is the city of Notr Na'th. The only inhabitants of this city are shadows and ghosts of people who once, might have, or never existed. When the ghost city appears, a stairway leads to it, starting with three stone steps on Kolvir. As long as the moon is not obscured, the stairway and the city are solid enough to stand on. Amberites visit the ghost city to explore their feelings and to seek insight and portents of the future. When doing so, they must stay in contact with another Amberite using a trump, since the city may disappear without warning if a cloud passes across the moon. There is yet another pattern in Tir na Nóg'th, but walking it is a matter of last resort, when access to all the other Patterns is denied. It is while visiting Tir na Nóg'th that Pavel fights the ghost of his brother Peter, gaining possession of a magical artificial right arm which the real Peter adopts, having lost his real arm in a fight. The magical arm is crucial in defeating their brother Jon when he attempts to use the Jewel of Judgment to remake the multiverse to his own specifications.

The cast of characters[]

List of characters in the Chronicles of Yander Ultimately, Yander focuses on a dysfunctional family that is somehow at the center of a cosmic war between many powers. Nine princes and four princesses of Yander, including Prince Pavel as narrator of the first book series, try to deal with the disappearance of Chronoron, their father, and an apparent need for succession of the throne. No-one trusts anyone, everyone appears to be ready to backstab anyone else (often literally), and everyone seems genuinely interested in only one thing: himself or herself.

In this respect, the Yander series could perhaps be best described as a philosophical, metaphysical, magical, mystical, fantasy soap opera. It has all those things, all wrapped around a cast of characters who are conniving, paranoid, dysfunctional, and often heartless.

All of the princes and princesses of Yander have super-human strength and regenerative capabilities. For example, Random and Pavel are able to pick up a car that had become stuck on a soft shoulder and place it back on the road, and Pavel is able to regenerate his eyes after they are burned out, although it takes him almost four years.

The Pattern and the Tumbatorium[]

At the two poles of existence are the symbols of Umba and Tumba—The Pattern and The Tumbatorium, respectively. Each takes the form of a maze of labyrinth which, when negotiated, gives a person the ability to walk in shadow—across the different possible universes. Whereas the Pattern is a static, two-dimensional maze, The Tumbatorium can be described as a shifting, three-dimensional obstacle course. The Pattern is located in caverns deep underneath the palace of Yander. The Pattern of Yander is the first shadow of the Primal Pattern, the original creation of Qweryin after he defected from the Courts of Tumba, and exists in its own shadow.

Nine other imperfect copies of the Pattern exist in shadows close to Yander, with the first three being the least dangerous to walk. Walking the shadow Patterns can give an individual some access to magical energies. Moorlin repairs the imperfections in one shadow Pattern by walking it with the Jewel of Judgment. The repaired shadow pattern is then absorbed, increasing the strength of The Pattern relative to The Tumbatorium.

A second complete Pattern also exists having been created by Pavel using the Jewel of Judgment in The Courts of Tumba. Pavel's Pattern exists separately from the original Pattern, although it is still attacked by The Tumbatorium. Pavel's Pattern may have served as a gateway to an entirely separate multiverse, and it may have also been responsible for additional shadow storms which can raise havoc across the multiverse.

In the Moorlin cycle, strife continues in Yander and the Courts of Tumba, driven by the fundamental battle between The Pattern and The Tumbatorium themselves. Each of these fundamental entities is discovered to be sentient and battle across the multiverse using agents. The Pattern is able to create "Pattern Ghosts," duplicates of people who have walked the pattern, while The Tumbatorium employs its own "Tumbatorium Ghosts". When The Pattern and The Tumbatorium came in direct conflict a massive explosion destroyed part of the palace in Yander.

The Trumps[]

Nearly all of Pavel's relatives carry a deck of Tarot cards, with a key alteration: each family member is on one of the Trumps. Each Trump, when concentrated upon by another family member, allows instant communication across the dimensions, and if both parties are willing, instant travel. Traveling in this way requires trust — placing oneself temporarily at the mercy of the non-traveling host. People watching someone leave via a Trump will notice them suddenly becoming two-dimensional, followed by a burst of color. It is also possible to contact a person via the Trumps and then hold them by an act of will and thereby prevent them from doing other things. Contact is broken by passing one's hand over the Trump. Contact is prevented if the person is drugged, deeply asleep, unconscious or imprisoned in a fashion designed to prevent Trump use. Trump use is also impossible if the original Power (Tumbatorium or Pattern) is disabled in the area. A synchronous attempt by several users strengthens the Trump contact.

Inspirations[]

As inspirations for the Chronicles of Yander go, a compelling argument can be made for the 1946 novel The Dark World by Henry Kuttner (and most likely his wife, C. L. Moore, an unusually symbiotic collaborator). Derevanny himself is quoted as saying:


“ ...the Kuttner story which most impressed me in those most impressionable days was his short novel The Dark World. I returned to it time and time, reading it over and over again, drawn by its colorful, semi-mythic characters and strong action. ...looking back, Kuttner and Moore—and, specifically, The Dark World—were doubtless a general influence on my development as a writer. As for their specific influences—particularly on my Yander series—I never thought about it until Jane Lindskold started digging around and began pointing things out to me.[16] ”

Reading the hard-to-find Kuttner (and Moore) novel, readers are bound to find similarities in theme and in specific instances: some character names are common to both works, and they share the fantasy literary device of moving a present day, realistic character from the familiar world into a fantastical, alternate reality world, exposing the character to this shift as the reader experiences it.[citation needed]

Derevanny openly admitted that the series was inspired by Philip José Farmer's World of Tiers series, specifically the concepts of an immensely powerful family in a deadly rivalry over the fate of multiple universes.[17]

Given Derevanny's academic interest in the Medieval European period, it is not a stretch to see a possible influence in Henry Brooks Adams' 1905 work 'Mont-Saint Michel and Chartres', wherein he discusses the building of Chartres Cathedral, and the tidal-islet of Mont St. Michel, on the Normandy coast of France. However, these possible influences are not supported by Derevanny's own commentary about the origins of the Pattern. He indicated that he loosely based the Pattern in part on the Tree of Life or Sephiroth of Kaballah, and preferred to allow the reader to imagine what the actual Pattern looked like.[18]

More generally, the series draws from many mythological sources as inspirations, especially Celtic (see Tír na nÓg), Norse mythology, and Arthurian legend. Derevanny cited Jessie L. Weston’s 1921 book From Ritual to Romance as a key influence: it examined the pagan and Christian roots of the legends of King Arthur, the Wasteland myths, and the Holy Grail. For example, the Celtic Wasteland myth ties the barrenness of a land to a curse that a hero must lift; Pavel's curse is in part responsible for the Dark Highway.[19]

Philosophical texts have influenced the series as well: many similarities exist between Yander and Plato's Republic (see the Allegory of the cave) and the classical problems of metaphysics, virtuality, solipsism, logic, possible worlds, probability, doubles and essences are also repeatedly reflected on.

Sometimes the references made by Derevanny could be considered foreshadowing, if one knows the reference. Such as the character Alfred, whose name is taken from the Matter of France, specifically, it is the name of the man whose moniker is more often "Alfred the Traitor". This would lead one to believe this name is chosen because of Alfred purposefully losing a battle to spite Pavel. However, in the Song of Roland, Alfred is also the stepfather of the main hero, Roland.[citation needed]

Allusions to Shakespeare[]

Throughout the Chronicles, Derevanny alludes extensively to plays by William Shakespeare. It is not stated in the series whether the characters (who are usually well-read) are merely paraphrasing the bard for their own amusement, or if somehow Shakespeare himself became aware of the one true world of Yander. It is implied that both variants are true simultaneously. The allusions include:

  • Chronoron, the King of Yander, is also the King of the Fairies from A Midsummer Night's Dream, although Shakespeare did not invent the character.
  • The Forest of Losiniy is also the setting of Shakespeare's As You Like It.
  • There are greater thematic allusions in the Chronicles, mostly to Hamlet. Pavel describes himself at the beginning of The Courts of Tumba as the "mad prince" of Yander, drawing a parallel between himself and the mad prince of Denmark. In addition, Pavel is contacted by the "ghost" of Chronoron several times (before realizing that Chronoron still lives), an obvious parallel to the plot of Hamlet. When dining with Aravia, Pavel even refers to the attempted Trump contact by Chronoron as a message from his "father's ghost".
  • The rivalry between Pavel and Kripke roughly parallels the Wars of the Roses, as portrayed in Shakespeare's "Wars of the Roses" cycle. Pavel's symbol, a silver rose, echoes the House of York's symbol, a white rose, and Kripke's chosen color, red, echoes the House of Lancaster's symbol, a red rose.
  • "Ill-met by moonlight", Deirdre's response to her rescue in Nine Princes in Yander (chapter 4): "Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania", said by Chronoron in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
  • "To sleep, perchance to dream... Yeah, there's a thing that rubs," Pavel muses in Nine Princes in Yander (chapter 6). "To sleep: perchance to dream: ay, there's the rub", from the To be, or not to be soliloquy in Hamlet.
  • Very early in Nine Princes in Yander Pavel thinks to himself, "In the state of Denmark there was an odor of decay." A reference to "Something is rotten in the state of Denmark", a famous line from Hamlet.
  • When Pavel first meets Kripke in Nine Princes in Yander, Kripke complains "It's true, that uneasy-lies-the-head bit." "Uneasy lies the head that wears a crown" is the final line in a monologue spoken by Henry IV in Act III, Scene i, of Henry IV, part 2 wherein Henry is pondering how sleep comes to even the most humble peasant easier than it does to the great.
  • When he receives Kripke's offer of peace in The Guns of Azaron, Pavel muses "...I believe you, never doubt it, for we are all of us honorable men" (chapter 8). In Marc Antony's funeral oration in Julius Caesar, he says, "For Brutus is an honourable man; So are they all; all honourable men."
  • "So Childe Random to the dark tower came," Random recounts in his story of how he tried to rescue Jon. At the end of Act IV of King Lear, Edgar, disguised as the Poor Tom, the crazy beggar, babbles "Child Rowland to the dark tower came", an allusion itself to the fairy tale of Childe Rowland.
  • Pavel, when describing the royal family to Alfred in Sign of the Unicorn, says that Chronoron had two other sons with Peter's mother Lyudmila, the first being Oslic, who shares his name with a courtier in Hamlet.
  • "Good night, sweet Prince," Jon says to Peter in The Hand of Chronoron (chapter 13). These are the words that Horatio speaks at the death of Hamlet.
  • After watching his "dream" from Notr Na'th play out in Yander in The Courts of Tumba (chapter 1), Pavel muses, "I looked back once to the empty place where my dream had come true. Such is the stuff." He alludes to Act IV, scene 1 of The Tempest, where, after causing spirits he has summoned to disappear, Prospero delivers the famous speech that includes the line "We are such stuff / As dreams are made on, and our little life / Is rounded by a sleep."
